articles.title: Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’
articles.author: Ben Brubaker
articles.body_markdown:
One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed.

Computer networks have grown much more reliable since that first test nearly 60 years ago. But we also demand a lot more of them. When you watch a movie online, the video data gets divided into a series of tiny “packets” that hop between way stations called routers on their way to your computer. Links between routers sometimes fail. One reason our videos aren’t constantly glitching out is that each router has a thorough contingency plan — a set of rules for redirecting packets in case a link goes down.

If a large outage cuts off every path between two points, there’s no way a packet can get through. But ideally, a network would be able to withstand any pattern of link failures short of this worst-case scenario. Researchers call this property “perfect resilience.” For over a decade, computer scientists have sought to understand what kinds of networks can be made perfectly resilient under realistic conditions.

Now, in a paper that was presented at the Symposium on Theory of Computing in June 2026, two researchers have settled the question with a comprehensive proof. They showed that there are exactly four minimal network structures that can thwart perfect resilience. In networks that lack these structures, you can always concoct rules that will reliably deliver packets from any source to any destination, regardless of which links fail.

“It’s a very elegant contribution,” said Michael Schapira, a computer scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who was not involved in the result. “It’s pretty rare that you get a complete understanding of something.”

## Think Globally, Act Locally

Imagine you have a network of routers in which each device can direct data packets bound for any other point in the network. You can then ask yourself: What instructions should the routers follow?

One simple approach would be to map out the shortest path between every pair of points in the network, and then give each router a copy of the map. If the network ever changes — if even a single link fails — start over and do it again.

In principle, this strategy will ensure that every packet reaches its destination. In practice, it’s far too slow. Calculating shortest paths is inherently a “global” problem — it requires knowledge of the entire network. In a real-world network, that calculation might take up to a few seconds. But each router has to act fast, in a fraction of a millisecond or less. That means routers must direct packets using only locally accessible information, such as the status of links to their immediate neighbors.

This restriction makes the problem of perfect resilience much more complicated. Without any global coordination between routers, packets might get trapped in loops.

In a 2012 paper, Schapira and five other researchers formally defined perfect resilience and devised a mathematical model to study when it’s achievable. They assumed that routing rules must have a simple form. A router can decide in which direction to send each new packet using only three factors: the packet’s destination, the link it arrived on, and which neighboring links have failed. The rules can’t depend on the path that a packet has taken so far, since routers don’t have access to this information.

With these assumptions, the researchers aimed to capture “something very close to how networks actually operate,” said Brighten Godfrey, a computer scientist at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign who co-authored the 2012 paper.

Godfrey, Schapira, and their colleagues showed that in this model, perfect resilience isn’t always achievable. They did so by finding a single example of a network layout that can’t be made perfectly resilient. No matter what set of routing rules you choose, there’s always a pattern of link failures that will cause some packets to get stuck in a loop.

But the network they identified was fairly complicated. Was it a rare example? Or is perfect resilience impossible in many other networks as well?

## Minor Problems

The 2012 paper caught the attention of Stefan Schmid, a networking researcher now at the Technical University of Berlin. He toyed with the perfect-resilience problem on and off for years, but his first real progress came in 2020, when he and his colleagues made a connection to a topic in mathematics called the theory of graph minors.

Computer scientists have long studied the mathematical properties of real-world networks by modeling them as graphs — webs of nodes connected by lines called edges. Imagine that you start with a graph, then repeatedly simplify it using three basic operations: You can delete a node, delete an edge, or merge pairs of connected nodes. The graphs that you can obtain by combining these operations are known as the minors of the larger graph.

Mark Belan/Quanta Magazine

These operations never make it more likely that packets will get routed in endless loops. If a graph is perfectly resilient, then so are all of its minors.

You can reverse this logic and understand the behavior of large, complex graphs using the properties of their simpler minors. An iconic result in graph theory, called the Robertson-Seymour theorem, tells you what you can learn from this kind of reversal. Applied to network resilience, the theorem states that there’s only a finite number of minors that are not perfectly resilient — every larger graph that lacks perfect resilience reduces to one of these so-called forbidden minors. If you can identify the full set of forbidden minors, you’ll have a complete understanding of when perfect resilience is achievable.

Unfortunately, the Robertson-Seymour theorem doesn’t tell you how many forbidden minors there are, or how to find them. “We know such a finite set exists,” said Matthias Bentert, a theoretical computer scientist at the Technical University of Berlin and Schmid’s collaborator on the new paper. “But we don’t know, does it contain one or two graphs, or does it contain 100,000 graphs?”

The researchers wanted to find the complete set of forbidden minors and prove that no others existed.

In their 2020 paper, Schmid and his colleagues identified two simple graph minors that prevent perfect resilience, but then they got stuck. Schmid suspected they’d need a collaborator with more expertise in graph theory to make further progress. Three years later, he met Bentert at a research retreat, and they worked together briefly on a different problem. In 2025, when Bentert was wrapping up a postdoctoral fellowship in Norway, Schmid invited him to join his group in Berlin.

“It was a really perfect match,” Schmid said. “Matthias made a lot of very fast contributions on a couple of our problems.” Perhaps he’d help make quick work of the perfect-resilience problem, too.

## Escaping the Maze

Bentert quickly identified a third forbidden minor. He then decided to see how far he could get by attacking the problem from the other direction. Perhaps if there were no additional forbidden minors — if the three they had found were the complete set — then he could prove that all graphs that lacked these three could be made perfectly resilient.

The strategy worked, but not in the way he had hoped. “I found that, actually, I cannot show it, because it’s not true,” Bentert said. He had discovered a fourth obstruction.

So now they had four forbidden graph structures. Were there more? Bentert tried the same strategy again: Prove that all graphs that lacked these four minors could be made perfectly resilient. The strategy worked, this time because he really had found the full set.

Bentert hadn’t expected the answer to be so simple. “I would have stopped if I reached 50 or so, but that it’s really only four was a little bit of a surprise to me,” he said.

Of course, knowing that perfect resilience is theoretically achievable for any given network is only useful if you know how to choose the right routing rules. Fortunately, Schmid and Bentert’s new result also yields a fast algorithm for finding these rules, which turn out to take a similar form in any network. They’re all based on a trick for escaping mazes: Simply take a right turn at every intersection. The only networks where a maze navigation–based approach fails are those containing one of the four forbidden minors. For those networks, changing the rules won’t help.

## Real-World Resilience

With their new result, Schmid and Bentert have fully resolved the perfect-resilience problem as it was originally posed in 2012. But the solution isn’t all good news. Even though there are only four graph structures that obstruct perfect resilience, the fact that they’re so simple means that many networks will have them as minors. Dense networks with many connections are especially likely to lack perfect resilience — an ironic outcome, given that adding more links to a network is the most straightforward way to make it more reliable.

“The more connectivity you have, the more possible subgraphs there are,” Godfrey said. “I wouldn’t be surprised if many real-world networks do not have a solution for perfect resilience.”

That may not be a deal-breaker: In some communication networks, resilience isn’t as critical as high speed and low congestion, two factors that Schmid and Bentert’s rules don’t take into account. And in cases where resilience is important, Schmid and Bentert’s result may not be the end of the story. They now plan to study how the situation changes if each packet can carry a record of the last few nodes it visited. Bentert is optimistic that this approach could make perfect resilience achievable for a broader range of networks, yet still remain feasible in the real world.

“Maybe some very freaky networks will not be perfectly resilient” even in a modified version of the problem, he said. “But everything that will ever be designed by a human or a machine will be.”

articles.title: Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
articles.author: Katie McQue
articles.body_markdown:
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.

"There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."

Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.

The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.

But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.

The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.

Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."

Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.

"There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented," the company warned investors.

### Anthropic's founders and employees just got very rich

Anthropic's corporate structure is intended to protect its mission, even as it pursues commercial success. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation (PBC), meaning its board must balance shareholder interests with its social mission.

As part of that structure, the company has installed an oversight body known as the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which has the power to appoint four of the company's seven directors. The founders effectively control the appointment of the remaining three.

The trust can, however, be dissolved. Doing so would require the approval of all seven co-founders, as well as a majority vote among shareholders with voting rights.

That arrangement could create a potential route for founders and shareholders to override the trust's influence over company decisions, legal experts interviewed for this article said.

"If there is a fight about some important safety decision, such as 'Are we satisfied that this super-advanced model is safe for users and society, or should we hold off for a couple of months to do extra tests or for whatever other safety reason?,' there's the possibility for the founders and the employees to basically ally against the trustee and neutralize their control rights," said Roberto Tallarita, an assistant professor at Harvard Law School.

The listing has also made many Anthropic employees wealthy. Each of the company's seven co-founders hold a stake in the company currently worth more than $20 billion. Its 5,300 employees hold an estimated $232 billion in combined equity. Non-founder employees were able to sell up to 10% of their holdings on the first trading day.

Those substantial financial stakes could influence how Anthropic's staff approaches decisions around safety and risk, said Tallarita.

"If they make decisions that are driven by safety considerations, but are bad for the bottom line, the stock price will react, and private investors will have reasons to exert some pressure on the company," he said.

The financial rewards could also change Anthropic's internal culture, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University.

"And now so many of these people will be multimillionaires too, which I think will just raise the temperature and egos and sense of stakes," Kreps said.

In his comments on Thursday, Amodei addressed these concerns.

"To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," he said. "Today puts the company in a stronger financial position and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing."

### Commercial and competitive pressures may compete with safety

Competition between AI companies is fierce.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman described the rivalry between major AI developers as a "race dynamic in the fog of war" while speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit this week.

That dynamic is "a bad thing," Altman said. "I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted."

OpenAI also plans to go public, and filed preliminary IPO paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, shortly after Anthropic. But Altman said in September the company has delayed those plans.

In an essay the same month, Amodei discussed the need for AI companies to carefully "pace" the development of frontier models.

"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless," Amodei wrote. "We have sought a middle way: to show that it's possible to build carefully and succeed commercially, and to make safety something on which AI companies compete."

"Anthropic has done a fairly good job of investing in analysis of what its models can and can't do, and the vulnerabilities that it creates, and publishing at least some version of this analysis," Kreps said.

In April, Anthropic announced that it would restrict access to its Claude Mythos model after internal testing revealed its powerful cybersecurity capabilities. The company said Mythos could identify and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers, making it a potential tool for hackers.

On June 9, less than three months later, Anthropic introduced Fable 5, a Mythos-class model, for general use with additional safeguards to restrict certain high-risk cyber, biological and chemical capabilities. The original Mythos model remains restricted to selected partners.

"In the past, the fact that the trust and the founders were aligned helped them delay the release of Mythos for several months," said Stavros Gadinis, faculty director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Business at the University of California Berkeley's law school. "But this was at a moment when they felt they were leading the pack."

Anthropic's decision to enter the defense contracting space has raised questions about how its commercial relationships align with its stated mission, said Kreps.

In November 2024, Anthropic announced a partnership with defense contractor Palantir, whose software is used in military intelligence and targeting operations. Under the agreement, Anthropic made its Claude models available to U.S. defense and intelligence agencies through Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform.

However, Anthropic earlier this year resisted allowing the Pentagon to use its technology for autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance. Negotiations broke down in February, resulting in the U.S. government designating Anthropic a "supply chain risk to national security."

"It does seem to raise a set of concerns about partnering with Palantir, which is contracting with the Pentagon for targeting. What part of that is AI for humanity?" said Kreps. "A lot of people who work there went there because safety was the guiding light."

### AI development is accelerating

Questions over Anthropic's promise to prioritize safety over commercial success are becoming more pressing as the technology itself advances. Anthropic is entering the public markets at a moment when its own research suggests the pace of AI development could be accelerating dramatically.

A November 2026 assessment by AI research nonprofit METR concluded that Anthropic's AI capabilities were improving at about twice the previous rate. Researchers estimate that a majority of this acceleration is now driven by Anthropic's use of AI tools to assist its own researchers. METR found no clear bottlenecks that might slow this progress, such as limits on data and computing power.

This could bring the company closer to a future in which increasingly capable AI systems help build even more advanced systems — a process known as autonomous recursive self-improvement. The prospect has fueled fears that Anthropic and other AI developers could lose control of their most advanced models, with potentially significant consequences for society.

"I'm scared myself, but it's very hard to imagine AI technology stopping or pausing," said Gadinis. "We are in a situation where these companies know better than anyone their models to the extent that someone understands them. So we have to work with them as a society."

### A federal regulatory vacuum

Society is left relying heavily on AI company executives to make consequential decisions about the risks posed by their own products, experts interviewed for this story said.

Since there are few government safeguards in place to shape how AI companies make decisions about safety and security, the industry's power is going largely unchecked, they said.

At the federal level, the AI sector remains largely unregulated. Under the second Trump administration, the White House has prioritized a deregulatory approach, seeking to limit federal oversight in favor of allowing AI labs to innovate without being encumbered by red tape.

In June, the White House announced its AI framework, which lets developers submit their newest models to federal agencies for cybersecurity and national security evaluations before release. However, the initiative is entirely voluntary.

"I don't think the government knows enough to regulate AI," said Tallarita. "This is a conversation that we should have as a political community, and probably the most serious conversation we should have right now."

"In the past, the fact that the trust and the founders were aligned helped them delay the release of Mythos for several months," said Stavros Gadinis, faculty director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Business at the University of California Berkeley's law school. "But this was at a moment when they felt they were leading the pack."
Anthropic's decision to enter the defense contracting space has raised questions about how its commercial relationships align with its stated mission, said Kreps.

In November 2024, Anthropic announced a partnership with defense contractor Palantir, whose software is used in military intelligence and targeting operations. Under the agreement, Anthropic made its Claude models available to U.S. defense and intelligence agencies through Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform.

However, Anthropic earlier this year resisted allowing the Pentagon to use its technology for autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance. Negotiations broke down in February, resulting in the U.S. government designating Anthropic a "supply chain risk to national security."

"It does seem to raise a set of concerns about partnering with Palantir, which is contracting with the Pentagon for targeting. What part of that is AI for humanity?" said Kreps. "A lot of people who work there went there because safety was the guiding light."
AI development is accelerating

Questions over Anthropic's promise to prioritize safety over commercial success are becoming more pressing as the technology itself advances. Anthropic is entering the public markets at a moment when its own research suggests the pace of AI development could be accelerating dramatically.

A November 2026 assessment by AI research nonprofit METR concluded that Anthropic's AI capabilities were improving at about twice the previous rate. Researchers estimate that a majority of this acceleration is now driven by Anthropic's use of AI tools to assist its own researchers. METR found no clear bottlenecks that might slow this progress, such as limits on data and computing power.

This could bring the company closer to a future in which increasingly capable AI systems help build even more advanced systems — a process known as autonomous recursive self-improvement. The prospect has fueled fears that Anthropic and other AI developers could lose control of their most advanced models, with potentially significant consequences for society.

"I'm scared myself, but it's very hard to imagine AI technology stopping or pausing," said Gadinis. "We are in a situation where these companies know better than anyone their models to the extent that someone understands them. So we have to work with them as a society."
A federal regulatory vacuum
Society is left relying heavily on AI company executives to make consequential decisions about the risks posed by their own products, experts interviewed for this story said.
Since there are few government safeguards in place to shape how AI companies make decisions about safety and security, the industry's power is going largely unchecked, they said.

At the federal level, the AI sector remains largely unregulated. Under the second Trump administration, the White House has prioritized a deregulatory approach, seeking to limit federal oversight in favor of allowing AI labs to innovate without being encumbered by red tape.

In June, the White House announced its AI framework, which lets developers submit their newest models to federal agencies for cybersecurity and national security evaluations before release. However, the initiative is entirely voluntary.

"I don't think the government knows enough to regulate AI," said Tallarita. "This is a conversation that we should have as a political community, and probably the most serious conversation we should have right now."

articles.title: Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology?
articles.author: Katie Worth
articles.body_markdown:
You see the promise on airline booking screens, shipping boxes, electronics and grocery aisles: “Carbon neutral.” “Net zero.” “Climate pledge friendly.” Those labels rest on the comforting premise that even when companies and countries keep burning fossil fuels, the resulting pollution can be canceled out by simply capturing the carbon and locking it away.

Recently, along with my colleagues at ProPublica and Drilled, I investigated how the world came to rely so heavily on this premise, particularly in the technology known as carbon capture and storage. CCS aims to trap carbon dioxide that would otherwise be warming the atmosphere and pump it thousands of feet below Earth’s surface, where, ideally, it stays put. The oil industry has long favored the idea.

At the industry’s prodding, the United Nations has effectively endorsed the idea that the technology can work at a massive scale.

Over the last two weeks, world leaders and negotiators met in Antalya, Turkey, for the U.N.’s annual flagship climate summit, where nations hash out global commitments to curb warming. A central foundation of these negotiations — and many of those carbon-neutrality labels and climate pledges — is the expectation that we can bury billions of tons of CO2 a year, an operation that would rival today’s entire global oil industry within just a couple of decades.

Yet our reporting found that expectation rests on thin evidence. After three decades of development, only 12 large-scale geologic storage projects have ever been built, and at least seven have underperformed or failed. Last year, the world buried less CO2 underground than a single large power plant emits annually.

Why do world leaders keep staking climate policy on a technology that remains unproven?

Because the models they all rely on to guide their approach have already presumed that it will work.

I spoke to more than 100 experts for this series, including several members of the wildly powerful group of people who build and run those models. Their simulations of the economy and environment map out how specific choices, like retiring coal plants or electrifying vehicles, could prevent warming catastrophic enough to submerge cities like Miami. Which means that if they’re wrong, Miami could pay the price.

One chart laid bare to me exactly how wrong they’ve been about CCS. It compares one prominent model’s projections for CCS with their projections for solar power, a technology so abundantly tested and proven that you can likely spot a panel out the nearest window:

### Carbon Capture Capacity Has Never Come Close to Projections

Meanwhile, solar electricity production has grown rapidly, far outpacing projections.

I wanted to understand what could possibly account for such a disparity. But the problem is the models are opaque: Unlike most scientists, who trade in public, peer-reviewed studies, modelers aren’t required to document every assumption they build into their influential simulations.

So I tracked down the leaders of the world’s three most influential climate models — one based in the Netherlands, another in Germany and a third in Austria — and asked. Here’s what I learned:

### Climate models assume it’s easy and efficient to capture carbon. It’s not.

Public data is hard to come by, but several analyses have found the real capture rates are far lower than the industry has promised. Yet the models calculate as much as a 92% success rate. When I pointed out this discrepancy to Keywan Riahi, who leads the Austrian model, he insisted that capturing concentrated CO2 from industrial emissions “is not high-tech, this is very easy to do.” Riahi told me the models assume a high rate of capture because they factor in incentives such as payouts from carbon taxes and large government subsidies. Add those incentives, he argues, and the capture rates would increase.

### They don’t account for problems that come up in real-world practice.

In project after project, operators have struggled to inject as much carbon into the earth as they say they can. For instance, at Chevron’s Gorgon natural gas processing plant in Australia, billed as the largest CCS operation on Earth, clogged wells and pressure spikes have forced operators to release most of their CO2 straight into the air. As it stands, only the German model, led by Jessica Strefler, assumed there’d be any limit to how much CO2 operators could inject underground at once. But, she told me, there is no good data to work from, and she pegged the limit based on “expert interviews” with people in the industry.

### They assume the Earth is a bottomless geologic landfill.

Modelers took that cue from a rosy 2005 U.N. report, which I’d learned had been written at the behest of Saudi Arabia and allied petrostates, that portrayed underground storage space as practically limitless. (The U.N.’s climate science body has said it stands by the report. Scientists who contributed to the report also defended their work. Authors and editors from Saudi Aramco, Chevron and Shell joined scientists in writing it; the companies did not respond to requests for comment.) Yet just last year, a paper in the journal Nature warned that the earth’s capacity to absorb CCS could be far more limited once you rule out pumping the gas beneath cities, into earthquake zones and under the deepest parts of the oceans. If CCS ever worked at the scale modelers imagine, the paper found, the Earth could run out of room as soon as early next century. Riahi, himself a co-author on that paper, conceded that although his model presumes the earth’s capacity for carbon storage is literally infinite, the real potential may be “smaller.”

### They assume that stored CO2 will stay put.

Scientists warn that even tiny annual leak rates over longtime horizons could undermine a storage site’s climate benefit. Our investigation found two large-scale sites that have leaked, one all the way to the surface. Surely the models all factor in this risk? I asked Detlef van Vuuren, leader of the Dutch model, if his did so. His one-word answer: “Nope.”

### The models all assume CCS gets more affordable over time, though real-world costs have steadily climbed.

When I asked Strefler if it makes sense to assume our children and grandchildren will pay big bucks to suck CO2 out of the air, even though today governments won’t spend pennies to avoid emitting that pollution, she said: “If a country is not willing to do that, I don’t see how they would be willing to” pay for CO2 removal.

In short, the modelers overlooked decades of underperformance, inflated capture rates, evidence of leaks and finite underground storage, all while assuming future generations will willingly bankroll an increasingly expensive industry. They pointed to a mix of legitimate studies to support those assertions. They also pointed to unreviewed white papers, casual chats with industry insiders and the 2005 U.N. report — of which van Vuuren was an author. Van Vuuren said his team is working to revise some of its assumptions, but he generally sees no technical reason why CCS cannot work, or should be excluded from the possibilities his model considers. He said it is a policy decision whether countries wish to invest the dollars and effort to make it happen.

One way to look at the model projections is as recipes for the future. Seen this way, the modelers’ argument is that their job is to assemble a cookbook, not tell us how each recipe tastes. In other words, the models merely show that if CCS works and is used at an extraordinary scale, it is possible to hit climate targets. And the modelers told ProPublica and Drilled that the delay in climate action has left few other tools to do so — and so they include CCS.

A good recipe, though, cannot rely on imaginary ingredients. If we’re making unrealistic assumptions, why not include the possibility that aliens will appear and hand us a solution to climate change, I asked Riahi, half joking.

“You can quote me that I think carbon dioxide removal is more likely than an alien,” Riahi said.

articles.title: One of Hilma af Klint’s Amazingly Rare Abstract Paintings Sold for a Record $12.7 Million at Auction. But Should It Have Been on Sale at All?
articles.author: Gabby Shell
articles.body_markdown:
On Thursday, a rare abstract painting by Swedish artist Hilma af Klint sold for a staggering $12.7 million at auction, raking in nearly 16 times its estimated worth. Painted in 1920, Ser III No. 5 is the first of af Klint’s abstract works to go to auction in over three decades, according to a statement from Bukowskis, the Stockholm-based auction house. But some critics say the sale defies the artist’s original intent.

Ser III No. 5 epitomizes af Klint’s late-career abstractions, exploring the idea of balance through its black-and-white background broken by a series of colorful, stacked geometric shapes. The painting works on “an intimate scale, steeped in af Klint’s mystical visual language,” Min Chen writes for ArtNet.

“She calls her work a message for humanity. There’s the balance of materialism but also spirituality,” Rachel Villari, author of Hilma af Klint’s Atom and The Tree of Knowledge, explains to NPR’s Rob Schmitz. “She was doing it as a way to convey a message for a future generation, [and] I believe we are that generation now”

Af Klint created her first abstract work in 1906 and over the course of her career amassed more than 1,200—but almost none have ever sold. Unlike many of her modern art contemporaries, af Klint refused to show off her works beyond her intimate circle.

For af Klint, her work was a way of connecting with a higher power; instead of hanging in a museum or private collection, she hoped her paintings would one day fill the walls of a temple. “For Hilma, this is a holy body of work,” Erik af Klint, the artist’s great grand-nephew and the board chair of the Hilma af Klint Foundation, tells Hyperallergic’s Rhea Nayyar.

Throughout her life, af Klint’s work was limited to a small, “spiritually interested audiences,” per the foundation’s website. Upon her death in 1944, af Klint, who never married or had children, bequeathed her collection to her nephew under the condition the public wouldn’t see them for at least 20 years. “The world, she believed, wasn’t ready for them,” Smithsonian’s Ellen Wexler wrote in May.

For decades, her works languished in relative obscurity until a 2018 Guggenheim exhibition propelled her into the public eye. Art historians deemed her to be the world’s first abstract artist, reclaiming the title from Wassily Kandinsky, and the 2022 biopic Hilma brought her story to the big screen.

But, even as interest in af Klint’s life and work rose, collectors couldn’t get their hands on any of her abstract pieces. The foundation still owns almost all of her pieces and guards them tightly. “Her spirituality and her mysticism are so appealing to people, but she’s been out of reach for so long,” Louise Wrede, head of Bukowskis’ art department, tells the Wall Street Journal’s Kelly Crow. Erik af Klint, in particular, has resisted calls to share, monetize or sell the work, Hyperallergic reports, believing the art should be available as a complete body of work to those seeking a spiritual experience.

Ser III No. 5 is one of the few exceptions. In 1992, an entity related to the foundation tried to sell four of Klint’s works to little avail, the Journal reports. In 1995, an unnamed collector purchased two, including Ser III No. 5, which his heirs recently decided to list for auction. Still, the final sticker price likely came as a surprise. Its high-end estimate was $800,000. Af Klint’s previous auction record, set in 2019, was a mere $165,825 for a 1931 watercolor titled The Power of the Spleen.

Villari tells NPR that af Klint’s resurgence in the artworld—coupled with the inaccessibility of her pieces—likely contributed to the pumped up price: “That makes it even more desirable to people who can afford to buy her work because what would you want more than the impossible painting that you’re not supposed to have or can’t have?”

Af Klint first began painting abstracts as a spiritual project. While in art school, she and four other young, female artists formed a group called “the Five,” devoted to spiritual beings they called the High Ones, per Bukowskis. Her first abstract series, The Paintings for the Temple, comprised 193 paintings dated from 1906 to 1913, each a fragment of an ideal spiritual temple.

Experts suggest af Klint wasn’t the only artist behind The Paintings for the Temple. She often worked closely with the other members of the the Five, including Anna Cassel, who is thought to have been painted some of the projects’ pieces.

Soon, she was introduced to Rudolf Steiner, an Austrian guru who founded the anthroposophy movement, which centers around the idea that the human consciousness can perceive spiritual worlds. In 1920, she began her next project, 85 geometric works including Ser III No. 5 meant to interpret the anthroposophy creed.

Villari tells NPR that it is hard to understand af Klint’s pieces, including Ser III No. 5 on their own. “I believe that her work should be kept together as a whole, and that they should be shown sequentially,” she says. “I know, from my own research, that looking at her work from beginning to end, you can see that it’s a progression of this message that they’re conveying.”

articles.title: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
articles.author: Ashley Lopez
articles.body_markdown:
A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.

It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.

Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.

If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.

There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.

"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.

Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.

So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.

One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.

And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.

Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.

And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.

### The practical and legal hurdles

Some legal scholars have observed that this agreement between states could run afoul of the compact clause in the Constitution, which says that "no state shall, without the consent of Congress … enter into any agreement or compact with another state … unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."

Norman Miller, a constitutional law professor at Willamette University, said that beyond the legal hurdles, he sees a range of practical issues with the compact.

Mostly, he said, it could upend what is a core feature of American presidential elections, which is that they are largely decentralized.

States individually decide who can vote and how they can vote. He said forcing electors from one state to vote according to the tallies in another state could create some tension.

"We would want to have a standardized, uniform set of rules regarding who gets to vote for president, how they vote, how those votes are tabulated, and to have a federal election authority doing that tabulation," he said. "I think trying to nationalize [the current system] and entrusting a national election to 51 separate election administrators would just sow discord and distrust."

But John Koza, the chairman of National Popular Vote, said if the compact works the way it is supposed to, none of that will be necessary.

"We don't need a centralized bureaucracy or a presidentially appointed commission that could be manipulated," he told NPR. "The simple fact is current state and federal law provide for the issuance of a certified vote count from each state. And all that has to be done is add them up."

But mostly, Miller said the biggest question before this effort is whether such a large reform should be done via a constitutional amendment.

Upending the Electoral College, some argue, would be a profound change to how the U.S. chooses the leader of the free world. Opponents of a national popular vote, such as Save Our States, argue that without the incentives created by the Electoral College, American politics will move more toward "toward more regional politics and would exacerbate existing divides."

Miller said even though it will be much more difficult to pull off, it would be worth going through a more fulsome process via Article 5 to get rid of the Electoral College, instead of working around it.

"This is where I think process matters," he said. "If you really want to have a national popular vote for the president and avoid all of the legal and practical difficulties, you need to do that through a constitutional amendment, because only a constitutional amendment can address the legal and practical challenges of conducting a national popular vote for the presidency."

A similar effort to pass an amendment to get rid of the Electoral College in 1969 failed, though. And very few amendments have even gotten close to passing in recent history.

Rosenstiel, the consultant to the National Popular Vote, said this is why he thinks groups like his are seeking a creative solution to something most Americans agree is a problem.

And, he said, he ultimately thinks a national popular vote will solve multiple problems at once. For one, he said, it will force presidential candidates to appeal to most of the country, as opposed to a select group of voters in battleground states.

And, importantly, he said, it would make all voters feel like their vote matters.

"We should have a system where every American citizen feels valued and is valued when they cast their vote," he said. "And there's only one reform that delivers it."

blocks.text: A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.
It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.

Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.

If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.

There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.

"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.

Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.

So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.

One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.
And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.

Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.
And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.
The practical and legal hurdles

Some legal scholars have observed that this agreement between states could run afoul of the compact clause in the Constitution, which says that "no state shall, without the consent of Congress … enter into any agreement or compact with another state … unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."
Norman Miller, a constitutional law professor at Willamette University, said that beyond the legal hurdles, he sees a range of practical issues with the compact.
Mostly, he said, it could upend what is a core feature of American presidential elections, which is that they are largely decentralized.
States individually decide who can vote and how they can vote. He said forcing electors from one state to vote according to the tallies in another state could create some tension.

"We would want to have a standardized, uniform set of rules regarding who gets to vote for president, how they vote, how those votes are tabulated, and to have a federal election authority doing that tabulation," he said. "I think trying to nationalize [the current system] and entrusting a national election to 51 separate election administrators would just sow discord and distrust."
But John Koza, the chairman of National Popular Vote, said if the compact works the way it is supposed to, none of that will be necessary.

"We don't need a centralized bureaucracy or a presidentially appointed commission that could be manipulated," he told NPR. "The simple fact is current state and federal law provide for the issuance of a certified vote count from each state. And all that has to be done is add them up."
But mostly, Miller said the biggest question before this effort is whether such a large reform should be done via a constitutional amendment.

Upending the Electoral College, some argue, would be a profound change to how the U.S. chooses the leader of the free world. Opponents of a national popular vote, such as Save Our States, argue that without the incentives created by the Electoral College, American politics will move more toward "toward more regional politics and would exacerbate existing divides."
